parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Penhale**
> 
> Penhale operates 22 hardware stores in country B. Head office sets each store's quarterly budget by taking the previous year's figures and adding 4%. Store managers receive a bonus if they meet their budget.
> 
> Store 7 is in a town that lost its bus route in February, and footfall fell by 19%. Its manager, Ilene, kept all staff on so customers were still served quickly. Store 14's manager met the budget by cutting staff hours.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows results for the two stores last quarter.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Penhale results, quarter ended June 2026**
> 
> |   | Store 7 | Store 14 |
> |---|---|---|
> | Labour cost variance (\$) | 31 000 adverse | 12 000 favourable |
> | Customer complaints | 11 | 47 |
> | Employees leaving | 0 | 2 |
> 
> Complaints at Store 14 rose from 9 to 47 in one quarter, and the two employees who left had each worked there for over ten years.
> 
> Marek, the finance director, argues that variances are the only fair way to compare 22 managers, because every store is measured in the same way.

Evaluate the usefulness of budget variances to Penhale in measuring the performance of its store managers.
parts.solution_md:
A variance is the difference between a budgeted figure and the actual result, and Penhale uses these differences to judge its store managers **[K]**. Store 7 reported a \$31 000 adverse labour variance while Store 14 reported \$12 000 favourable **[Ap]**. Taken alone the figures rank Ilene as the weaker manager, yet her town lost its bus route and footfall fell 19%, a change she could not influence and could not have foreseen when the budget was set **[An]**. Measuring her against a target built on last year plus 4% charges her with the consequences of an event outside her control, which tells Penhale nothing about how well she managed **[An]**

Store 14 shows the same weakness from the other direction **[K]**. Its manager met budget by cutting staff hours, and complaints rose from 9 to 47 while two employees of more than ten years' standing resigned **[Ap]**. The variance records the saving because it is a cost, but not the recruitment and training needed to replace experienced staff, nor the customers who may not return **[An]**. Penhale is therefore paying a bonus for a decision that has probably reduced the store's profit over a longer period than the quarter being measured **[An]**

Variances are not useless, however **[E]**. They are consistent across all 22 stores, cheap to produce and available quickly, and no realistic alternative measures 22 managers as promptly **[E]**. The problem is not the variance but that Penhale treats it as the whole answer, since a variance identifies where results differ from plan and was never designed to explain why **[E]**. Penhale should keep variances as the starting point and require each to be investigated before any bonus is decided, separating causes managers control from those they do not **[E]**. Adding a small number of non-financial measures, such as complaints and staff turnover, would also stop a manager improving one figure by damaging another, which is the precise failure Store 14 illustrates **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Brayford Events**
> 
> Brayford Events hires out marquees and staging for weddings and festivals in country T. Demand is highly seasonal, with 62% of annual revenue earned in four months.
> 
> Brayford sets one fixed budget each year. Last year's was built on 480 bookings; the business actually took 611. Every cost centre reported an adverse variance, and managers argued the figures told them nothing they could use.
> 
> Priya, the operations director, wants Brayford to move to flexible budgets so costs are compared at the level of bookings actually achieved.
> 
> Sam, the finance manager, is not convinced. Brayford's marquee crew of 26 are on annual salaries and are paid whether or not there is work, while transport and casual labour rise with each booking. Some costs, such as vehicle servicing, are partly fixed and partly variable. Brayford employs one part-time accountant, who already works two days a week.

Evaluate whether Brayford Events should replace its fixed budget with a flexible budget.
parts.solution_md:
A flexible budget is restated at the level of activity actually achieved, so costs are compared on a like-for-like basis **[K]**. Brayford budgeted for 480 bookings and took 611 **[Ap]**. Under a fixed budget almost every variable cost was certain to exceed its target simply because 27% more work was done, which is why every cost centre showed an adverse variance and managers dismissed the figures **[An]**. Flexing removes that distortion, leaving variances that reflect price and efficiency, so Brayford could see whether casual labour actually cost more per booking rather than only that it cost more in total **[An]**

The gain is largest in a business this seasonal **[K]**. Brayford earns 62% of revenue in four months **[Ap]**. A single annual budget spread across twelve months bears little relation to what any individual month should cost, so a manager working through the peak is judged against an average that never described their workload **[An]**. Flexed monthly figures would give each period a target built on its own volume, making the comparison fair and the variance worth investigating **[An]**

The obstacles are real, however **[E]**. Flexing requires costs to be split reliably into fixed and variable, and Brayford's do not divide cleanly; 26 salaried crew are fixed whatever the volume, while vehicle servicing is partly both **[E]**. If those splits are estimated badly the flexed budget will be wrong, and a confidently wrong variance is more dangerous than an obviously useless one, because managers will act on it **[E]**. There is also the question of who does the work, since one accountant working two days a week must produce the restatements on top of existing duties **[E]**. On balance Brayford should still move to flexible budgets, but begin only with the costs that clearly vary, such as transport and casual labour, leaving salaried crew in a fixed block **[E]**. That captures most of the benefit at the volumes which caused the problem, without asking a part-time accountant to model costs nobody has yet separated accurately **[E]**

With 611 bookings against a budget of 480, adverse variances were almost automatic, and flexing removes that volume distortion so the remaining variances reflect price and efficiency rather than how much work was done. However, flexing depends on splitting costs reliably into fixed and variable, and Brayford's do not divide cleanly
> - Managers have dismissed the current figures as telling them nothing they can use, so the budget has already lost its value as a control. However, a flexed budget that rests on badly estimated cost splits could be worse, since a confidently wrong variance will be acted on where an obviously useless one is ignored
> - With 62% of revenue earned in four months, an annual budget spread evenly across twelve describes no individual month accurately, and a manager working the peak is judged against an average that never described their workload. However, monthly flexing multiplies the work twelvefold for one accountant working two days a week

> - Brayford could flex only the clearly variable costs and leave salaried crew in a fixed block, capturing most of the benefit at far lower risk. However, this leaves semi-variable costs such as vehicle servicing unaddressed, so some distortion would remain
> - The underlying problem may be forecasting rather than budgeting, since a budget built on 480 bookings underestimated demand by 27%. However, improving the forecast would not fix the unfairness of comparing costs at one volume against a budget set for another
>

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Draycott**
> 
> Draycott supplies and services commercial kitchen equipment for restaurants and hotels in country F. Nadia founded the business alone and it now employs 54 people across four departments.
> 
> Two years ago Draycott nearly closed. Spending on new vans went ahead without any check while a large customer delayed payment, and Nadia had to sell equipment to meet the wage bill. She introduced departmental budgets shortly afterwards.
> 
> Nadia is now unsure they are worth keeping. Each of the four managers spends around three days a quarter preparing budget submissions. Last year two departments underspent by \$22 000 and \$14 000, which Nadia believes shows they asked for more than they needed. Revenue is growing at about 30% a year, so figures agreed in January are often out of date by June.
> 
> Her accountant has suggested replacing budgets with a monthly review of management accounts.

Evaluate whether Draycott should stop using budgets.
parts.solution_md:
A budget is a financial plan setting agreed targets for income and spending over a period **[K]**. Draycott's four managers each spend around three days a quarter preparing submissions **[Ap]**. That is roughly 48 management days a year in a business of 54 people, and in a firm growing at 30% a year those days have an obvious alternative use in winning and servicing customers **[An]**. The case is stronger still because figures agreed in January are out of date by June, so managers are held to targets the business has already outgrown **[An]**

The underspends point to a second problem **[K]**. Two departments came in \$22 000 and \$14 000 below budget **[Ap]**. Nadia reads this as managers overstating their needs, and if she is right the budgets are not controlling spending but recording inflated requests, which makes the process misleading as well as slow **[An]**. A budget nobody expects to be accurate stops being a control and becomes an administrative routine **[An]**

Against this, the reason budgets exist at Draycott has not gone away **[E]**. The business nearly closed because van spending went ahead unchecked while a customer delayed payment, and it was the absence of any approval process, not a faulty one, that caused it **[E]**. Monthly management accounts report what has already been spent, whereas a budget sets a limit before the money leaves; the two do different jobs, and the accountant's proposal replaces control with reporting **[E]**. Draycott should keep budgets but change them, moving to quarterly figures so they keep pace with 30% growth and cutting the submission process down so it costs days rather than weeks **[E]**. Abandoning them entirely would remove the one safeguard introduced precisely because its absence almost ended the business **[E]**

However, quarterly budgeting means four rounds of submissions a year rather than one, which could increase the management time it is meant to save unless the process is genuinely simplified
>

> **[case-study]**
> **Tavener Roofing**
> 
> Tavener Roofing installs roofs on new houses in country M. It sets budgets each quarter and reviews variances at the end of each one.
> 
> Tavener changed its roof tile supplier at the start of the quarter to one charging 15% less. Since then 1 in 9 roofs has needed tiles replaced after installation, and teams have spent time returning to completed jobs.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows Tavener's variances for the quarter ended June 2026.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Tavener Roofing variances, quarter ended June 2026**
> 
> |   | Variance (\$) |
> |---|---|
> | Revenue | 12 000 adverse |
> | Materials | 9 000 favourable |
> | Labour | 15 000 adverse |

Analyse **two** ways in which variance analysis could help Tavener Roofing to improve its performance.
parts.solution_md:
Variance analysis compares actual results against budget and identifies where the difference lies **[K]**. Tavener's figures show a \$9 000 favourable materials variance alongside a \$15 000 adverse labour variance in the same quarter **[Ap]**. Reading the two together points to the change of tile supplier, because the cheaper tiles saved money on materials while the rework caused by 1 in 9 roofs failing pushed labour hours above budget **[An]**. Without the variances Tavener would see only that profit was down; with them it can identify the supplier as the cause and either switch back or renegotiate, removing a \$15 000 problem in order to keep a \$9 000 saving **[An]** Variance analysis also allows Tavener to act within the period rather than after it **[K]**. Variances are currently reviewed quarterly, and the adverse revenue variance stands at \$12 000 **[Ap]**. Calculated monthly instead, a shortfall in roofs completed would appear after four weeks rather than three months, so Tavener could redeploy teams or chase new contracts while the quarter still had time to recover **[An]**. parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Merrick Laundry**
> 
> Merrick Laundry washes and presses bed linen and towels for hotels in country R. It employs 140 people.
> 
> Merrick has used incremental budgeting for nine years. Each department's budget is the previous year's figure increased in line with inflation.
> 
> The marketing budget still includes \$18 000 a year for advertising in printed hotel directories, although 84% of new customers now arrive through an online booking platform. The maintenance budget has not risen in real terms since 2019, and machine breakdowns rose from 14 to 31 last year.
> 
> Rashida, the finance director, wants Merrick to move to zero budgeting. The operations manager has warned that departmental managers are already stretched.

Analyse **two** benefits to Merrick Laundry of introducing zero budgeting.
parts.solution_md:
Zero budgeting requires every budget to start at zero, so managers must justify all spending from scratch rather than inheriting last year's figure **[K]**. Merrick's marketing budget still carries \$18 000 a year for printed directory advertising while 84% of new customers arrive through an online platform **[Ap]**. Under incremental budgeting that \$18 000 is never questioned, because it is simply uprated each year, whereas zero budgeting would force the marketing manager to argue for it against competing uses of the money **[An]**. Spending that can no longer be justified would be removed, releasing \$18 000 to be redirected to the channel actually generating customers, so the same total budget produces more new business **[An]** A second benefit is that zero budgeting moves funds towards areas of genuine need **[K]**. Merrick's maintenance budget has not risen in real terms since 2019 while breakdowns have more than doubled from 14 to 31 **[Ap]**. Incremental budgeting cannot correct this, because it fixes each department's share at whatever it happened to be, so an underfunded department stays underfunded however much its workload changes **[An]**. Starting from zero would let the maintenance case be judged on current evidence, and if breakdowns fall Merrick avoids the lost output and emergency repair costs of machines failing while hotels are waiting for their linen **[An]** > **[mark-scheme]** > - An 8-mark analyse question requires two developed points, each with knowledge of a relevant concept, applied to the business context, and followed by a chain of reasoning that explains the causes, impacts or consequences for the business > - This is a 'Level of response' answer where the examiner judges how well you have displayed the key skills of knowledge, application and analysis > > | **Level** | **Knowledge** | **Application** | **Analysis** | > |---|---|---|---| > | **2** | **2 marks**

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Denby**
> 
> Denby makes cardboard boxes for food producers in country J. Its budget for the year was prepared on the assumption that it would produce 40 000 boxes.
> 
> Demand was stronger than expected and Denby actually produced 46 000 boxes.
> 
> Table 1.1 shows Denby's budgeted and actual figures for the year.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Denby budgeted and actual figures**
> 
> |   | Budget | Actual |
> |---|---|---|
> | Output (boxes) | 40 000 | 46 000 |
> | Variable production costs (\$) | 128 000 | 151 800 |
> | Fixed costs (\$) | 50 000 | 50 000 |
> 
> The finance director wants the budget flexed to the actual level of output before any variance is reported.

Calculate Denby's flexed budget for variable production costs and the resulting variance.
parts.solution_md:
**Variance = \$4,600 adverse ****[4]**

**Method**

Budgeted variable cost per box

`equals space fraction numerator $ 128 comma 000 over denominator 40 comma 000 end fraction space equals space $ 3.20` **[1]**

Flexed budget for variable production costs

`equals space 46 comma 000 cross times $ 3.20 space equals $ 147 comma 200` **[1]**

Variance = Actual − Flexed budget

`equals $ 151 comma 800 minus $ 147 comma 200 space equals $ 4 comma 600 space adverse space open parentheses straight A close parentheses` **[2]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Up to 3 marks for valid workings
> - 4 marks for the correct answer of \$ 4,600 A
> 
> A correct answer with no working shown still receives full marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Work out the cost per unit before you flex anything. Comparing the actual \$151,800 with the original budget of \$128,000 gives a variance of \$23,800 adverse, which looks alarming but is mostly just the cost of making 6,000 extra boxes the budget never allowed for. Flexing strips out the effect of volume, so what remains is the part management can actually do something about.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** way in which budgets can help a business to allocate its resources.
parts.solution_md:
Allocating resources means deciding how limited finance is divided between the competing demands of different parts of the business **[1]**. Setting budgets forces those claims to be compared against one another before any money is committed, so a department expecting to grow can be given a larger share than one whose workload is falling **[1]**. Because every request is justified at the same time, spending is directed towards the areas that contribute most to the objectives rather than to whichever manager asks first **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Allocating resources means dividing limited finance between competing uses within the business
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Budgeting forces competing claims to be compared before money is committed
> - Departments can be funded in line with expected workload or contribution rather than by habit
> - Spending is directed to the areas that support the business objectives most closely
> - Zero budgeting strengthens this further by requiring each claim to be justified from scratch
> - Setting limits in advance stops one department consuming finance needed elsewhere
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Allocate" means choosing between competing claims, so your answer needs at least two claims in it. If what you have written would make just as much sense in a business with a single department, you have explained planning rather than allocation. Naming two parts of the business pulling on the same money is the quickest way to show you understand the term.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** drawback to a business of using budgets.
parts.solution_md:
A budget sets an agreed spending limit for a manager over a fixed period **[1]**. One drawback is that this can encourage unhelpful behaviour, such as a manager spending what remains of an allocation near the year end simply to avoid a smaller budget next time **[1]**. Money then goes on things the business does not need in order to protect a department's position, so the budget drives decisions that reduce profit rather than controlling costs as intended **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A budget is a financial plan setting agreed targets for income and spending over a period
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Budget holders may spend up to their limit unnecessarily to protect next period's allocation
> - Managers may deliberately overstate their requirements when budgets are negotiated
> - Budgets set in advance become unrealistic if trading conditions change, making them a poor guide
> - Rigid budgets may block worthwhile spending that arises after the budget was agreed
> - Preparing and monitoring budgets takes management time and can create conflict between departments
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The strongest budget drawbacks are about people, so put a person in your answer. "Budgets are inflexible" is a statement; "a manager spends the rest of the allocation in March so the budget is not cut next year" is an explanation, because it names who acts and why. Behaviour is far easier to develop into a chain of reasoning than a general criticism.

parts.problem_md: Explain why a favourable variance is not always good news for a business.
parts.solution_md:
A favourable variance means the actual result was better for profit than the budget planned **[1]**. However, the reason behind it may be damaging; raw material costs below budget could mean cheaper, lower-quality inputs have been bought **[1]**. The saving appears immediately in this period's figures, while the cost of returns, complaints and lost repeat custom appears later, so a favourable variance can hide a problem rather than signal success **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A favourable variance occurs where the actual result is better for profit than the budgeted figure
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Lower costs may result from cheaper, poorer-quality materials, damaging quality and reputation
> - Underspending on training, maintenance or marketing flatters this period's figures but weakens future performance
> - A large favourable variance may show the budget was set too easily, making it a poor target rather than good performance
> - Higher revenue than budgeted may come from unplanned discounting the business cannot repeat
> - A favourable variance in one department may have been achieved by shifting costs or work onto another
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question says "not always", it is asking you to argue against the obvious answer. There is no credit for explaining why a favourable variance is normally welcome, however well written. Go straight to the case where it is not, and give the reason behind the figure, because that reason is where the marks sit.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** benefit to a business of using a flexible budget rather than a fixed budget.
parts.solution_md:
A flexible budget is adjusted to the level of output the business actually achieved **[1]**. This means costs are compared at the same activity level, so a manager whose department produced more than planned is not judged against a spending limit set for lower output **[1]**. The variances that remain then show genuine differences in efficiency or price rather than differences in volume, so the business can investigate the right problems instead of chasing figures that were always going to move **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A flexible budget restates budgeted figures at the actual level of output achieved
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Variances are no longer distorted by output being higher or lower than planned, so they show real performance
> - Managers are judged on factors within their control, which is fairer and more motivating
> - Investigation time is spent on genuine problems rather than on differences caused by volume alone
> - The business gets a more accurate picture of costs where demand is seasonal or hard to predict
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a three-mark Explain the third mark is almost always the consequence. Many answers name the benefit, describe it, then stop, which is two marks. Finish by saying what the business can now do differently: make a better decision, avoid a cost, act sooner. That final step is what turns a description into an explanation.

An adverse variance is the difference between a budgeted figure and an actual figure **[1]** where the actual outcome leaves the business worse off than planned, such as costs above budget or revenue below budget **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A variance where the actual result is worse for profit than the budgeted figure
> - Occurs when actual costs exceed budgeted costs, or actual revenue falls below budgeted revenue
> - The opposite of a favourable variance, which improves profit compared with the plan
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Adverse does not simply mean the number went up. A revenue figure below budget is adverse even though it is a smaller number, and a cost figure below budget is favourable. The word describes the effect on profit, not the direction of the figure, so decide first whether the item is a cost or a revenue.

A flexible budget is one that is adjusted to reflect the actual level of output or activity achieved **[1]**, so that budgeted costs and revenues rise or fall in line with how much the business has really produced or sold **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A budget that changes with the level of activity, so figures are restated at the output actually achieved
> - A budget in which variable costs are set per unit rather than as a fixed total, allowing the plan to move with volume
> - A budget designed so performance is compared at the same level of output, rather than against a plan built for a different volume
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any budget can be changed, so "a budget that can be changed" does not earn the marks. Say what the budget flexes with. The whole point of a flexible budget is that it moves with output, which is what makes a fair comparison possible when sales turn out higher or lower than planned.

An incremental budget takes the previous period's budget as its starting point **[1]** and adjusts it up or down by a set amount or percentage to give the figure for the new period **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - A budget set by taking the previous period's figures and adding or subtracting a small amount, rather than starting again from zero
> - A method in which the existing budget forms the base, with changes made only at the margin
> - A budget built by adjusting the current allocation, often for inflation or expected growth
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Every budgeting method is a financial plan for future spending, so writing that alone earns nothing here. The mark is for what separates this method from the others, and that is the starting point: last period's budget rather than zero. If your definition would read equally well for zero budgeting, it is not yet a definition of this one.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one **benefit to a business of using budgets.
parts.solution_md:
A budget is a financial plan for the future that helps a business control its performance **[1]**. One benefit is that it allows managers to compare actual results against targets using variance analysis **[1]**. For example, a retail business could quickly spot that its labour costs are higher than budgeted and take action before this seriously affects its profit **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A budget is a detailed financial plan for the future, which can be used to help control and monitor a business's performance.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Budgets allow a business to compare actual results against targets, using variance analysis to identify areas that need management attention - for example, a retail business could spot that its labour costs have exceeded budget and investigate why.
> - This system of budgeting also increases accountability, as individual budget holders, such as department managers, become responsible for staying within their own budgets, which can motivate them to control spending more carefully.
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Dayo's Bakery (DB)**
> 
> Dayo started a bakery business five years ago in country W. She uses batch production to make a range of breads, pastries and cakes, which she sells to local restaurants and retail outlets. DB now employs 18 workers. Skilled bakers are difficult to find in country W, as many have moved to work for larger food manufacturers in the capital city. Dayo uses on-the-job training to develop new employees, but this takes time and has increased costs.
> 
> Dayo has set a mission to 'provide high-quality, locally sourced baked goods to the communities of country W'. She plans to open a third bakery location by the end of the year.
> 
> DB does not have enough working capital to open the third location without additional finance. Two options are available:
> 
> - **Option A**: A bank loan of \$80 000 at an annual interest rate of 8%
> - **Option B**: A business partner, Kofi, who would invest \$80 000 in return for a 30% share of DB's annual profits
> 
> Table 1.1 shows DB's budgeted and actual financial data for the six months ended March 2024.
> 
> **Table 1.1 DB budgeted and actual financial data (six months ended March 2024)**
> 
> |   | Budget (\$) | Actual (\$) | Variance (\$) |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | Revenue | 120 000 | 105 000 |   |
> | Labour costs | 42 000 | 52 000 |   |
> | Raw material costs | 36 000 | 33 000 |   |
> | Fixed overheads | 18 000 | 18 000 | 0 |
> | **Total costs** | **96 000** | **103 000** |   |
> | **Profit** | **24 000** | **2 000** |   |

Calculate the variance in revenue and the variance in labour costs for DB.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Revenue variance = \$15,000 adverse**

**Final answer:** **Labour cost variance = \$10,000 adverse**

**Method**

$\text{Variance}=\text{Actual - Budget}$

Revenue variance

`equals space $ 120 comma 000 space minus space $ 105 comma 000 space

equals space $ 15 comma 000 space adverse space left parenthesis straight A right parenthesis`

Labour cost variance

`equals space $ 52 comma 000 space minus space $ 42 comma 000 space

equals space $ 10 comma 000 space space adverse space left parenthesis straight A right parenthesis`

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - Up to 2 marks for valid workings
> - 2 marks for the correct answer of `$ 15 comma 000 space straight A space and space $ 10 comma 000 space straight A`
> 
> A correct answer with no working shown still receives full marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you clearly label each variance as either 'adverse' (A) or 'favourable' (F). Many students calculate the correct figure but lose marks by not stating whether the variance is adverse or favourable. For revenue, if actual is lower than budget, this is adverse. For costs, if actual is higher than budget, this is also adverse — costs being higher than expected is bad for the business. Always show your working, including the formula, as this can earn you a mark even if your final answer is incorrect.

parts.solution_md:
A budget is a financial plan that sets targets for income and spending over a set period **[1]**. For DB, comparing actual figures against the budget shows that labour costs were \$10,000 higher than planned **[1]**. This helps Dayo see where costs are going wrong, which is useful information when deciding whether DB can afford a bank loan or a partner like Kofi to fund the new bakery location **[1]**

>

> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
>

> 
> AO1
> 
> - A budget is a financial plan setting targets for income and/or expenditure over a specific future time period.
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Because a budget sets targets in advance, it allows DB to compare actual results against the plan and spot where corrective action is needed - for example, Dayo's actual labour costs of \$52,000 were much higher than the \$42,000 budgeted, which the budget helps highlight as an area to investigate.
> - A budget gives Dayo a structured financial plan, helping her judge whether DB can afford to take on a bank loan or share profits with Kofi to fund the new third location.
>

A developed application point — one that goes beyond a simple statement and shows a chain of reasoning connected to the scenario — will earn you 2 marks rather than 1. Zero budgeting is when a business sets each budget back to zero every year **[1]**, meaning managers must justify their spending from scratch rather than basing it on the previous year's budget **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - An approach to budgeting that sets budgets to zero each year, rather than basing them on the previous year's figures, requiring budget holders to justify their budget from scratch each time
> - A budgeting method where every cost must be justified for each new period, rather than simply adjusting the previous budget
> - A method where budget holders start at zero and must argue for the funding they need each year, rather than automatically carrying over previous allocations
> 
> Accept all valid responses.
